summary: The assessee, a Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to wealth tax on the valuation date. The Wealth Tax Officer, Wealth Tax Officer assessed the assessee to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67, 1966 68, 1966 68 and 1967 68, but the Wealth Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that the assessee had not maintained any accounts of the assessee. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Assistant commissioner confirmed the order of the Wealth Tax officer. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the assessee was not entitled to any deduction under section 27(1) of the Wealth tax Act, wealth tax was not chargeable to wealth tax. The Tribunal further held that the assets of the assessee were not exempt from wealth tax under section 27 of the Wealth Act, wealth Tax Act, wealth of the assessee was liable to be included in the net wealth of the assesee. The Tribunal also held that the wealth tax was chargeable to wealth Tax on the valuation dates. The Tribunal, however, held that the Wealth Tax Act, Wealth Tax Act and Wealth Tax Act were not chargeable to Wealth Tax Act. The Tribunal accordingly allowed the appeal. The Tribunal took the view that the assets were not exempt under section 27 (1) of Wealth Tax Act because the assessee had maintained the accounts of the assesees on accrual basis. The Tribunal observed that the assets had been acquired by the assessee on accrual basis and the assessee had been assessed to wealth Tax for the assessment year 1965 66, 1967 68, 1966 69 and 1967 68. The Tribunal found that the assets acquired by the assesee were not exempt on accrual basis under section 27. The Tribunal was of the view that since the assets were acquired by the assesses on accrual basis, the assets were liable to be excluded from the net wealth. The Tribunal did not accept the view taken by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the assets which were acquired by it on accrual basis were not exempt. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The assets which were purchased by the assessee were liable to wealth tax under the Wealth Tax Acts. [701B] 2. The assets were not exempted from wealth tax. [702C] 3. The assets are not exempt from Wealth Tax Act as they were not assets of the assesses. [705E] 6. The assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on account of the assessee, were not exempt or the assessee was assessed to Wealth Tax. [706E] 7. The assets had been purchased by the assesse on accrual basis on accrual basis in the open market. The assets belonged to the assessee and were not exempt, on accrual basis from wealth tax, but were not exempt as they were assets of the assessees. [707E] 7A] 8. The assets belonging to the assesee are not exempt. The assets belong to the assessee. [708E] 9. The assets belongs to the assessee, and are not exempt, but are not exempt under the Wealth tax. [807E] 9A] 10. The assets have been acquired by a Hindu Undivided family, and are neither exempt nor the assessee is assessed to wealthtax. [709E] 10. In the present case, the assets belong to a Hindu Undivided Hindu Family. The assets vest in the assessee. It is not in the hands of the assessee and the assets vest in him. [710E] 10A] 10A.

The plaintiff, who was a deemed tenant, filed a suit for possession of the suit property on the ground that he was a deemed purchaser of the suit land on or after 1st July, 1962. The plaintiff alleged that he was in possession of the land on or before 1st July 1962 and, therefore, he was entitled to be heard and decided by the Civil Court. The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The plaintiff filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the suit was barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore the question of the applicability of the provisions of Order 2 Rule 3 of the Code was not open to the Civil Court to decide the same. The High court, therefore, dismissed the second appeal. The appellant has come to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have jurisdiction to decide the question of tenancy. The question whether the tenancy is a deemed tenant or a deemed tenant is a question of fact which is by or under the Act required to be determined for grant or dealing with any question which is by and under the Act. [832D] 2. The question of tenancy is a mixed question of fact and law and it is not open to a Civil Court to go into the question whether the tenant is a deemed purchaser or a deemed purchaser. [833E] 3. The question as to whether the tenancy was a deemed tenancy or a deemed tenancy was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was expressly barred by Order II Rule 2(2) of the Civil Courts Procedure. [834F] 4. The question is whether the tenancy in question was a deemed purchase within the meaning of Section 58(2) and the Civil Court had jurisdiction to decide that question. [835G] 5. The question, whether the tenancy of the appellant was a deemed sale within the meaning ofs. 58(2), is a mixed issue of fact and fact and, therefore it was not open for a Civil Court, to decide the said question. [820H] 6. The question that arises for consideration is whether the appellant was in possession on or after the 1st July of 1962 and, if so, whether the suit was within the meaning Of section 58(2). [834G] 7. The question which arises for consideration in this case is whether the suit is barred by Order I Rule 2(1) of the C.P.C. or not. [836G] 8. The question referred to the High Court is whether the plaintiff was a deemed landlord within the meaningof section 58(1) and the suit was not barred by Order 1 Rule 2(4) of the Act. The High C.P., and the Courts below have not committed any error in holding that the suit is not barred by the principle of res judicata. [837F] 9. The question was whether the suit filed by the plaintiff was barred by the principles of res judicata or not. The question arose whether the suit could be decided by a Civil Court. [838G] 10. The question before the High C. P. and the Courts was whether the plaintiff had a right to be heard in the suit. [839G] 11. The question raised before the High court was whether the appellant had a right of tenancy under section 58(3) and the question was whether he was a tenant or a tenant. The High, Court, however, held that the appellant was not a deemed tenant. [840G] 12. The question in the present case was whether the tenancy under section 8(2) was a deemed lease within the meaning thereof. [841G] 13.

The petitioners were engaged in the construction industry in the year 1986. They were engaged in construction work in the year 1987. They were paid the minimum wages payable to such workmen. The Corporation has fixed the minimum wages as payable to such employees in the year 1988. The petitioners were engaged as carpenters in the construction work in Government service. They were also paid the minimum wage as payable to the carpenters. The Corporation, however, fixed the minimum wage payable to such carpenters as was payable to such persons. The petitioners' case was that the Corporation has fixed minimum wages payable for such carpenter in Government service and, therefore, the petitioners are entitled to the same wages as were paid to such carpenter or craftsmen. The Corporation filed a counter affidavit in which it was stated that the petitioners were engaged on daily rated basis in the construction department of the Corporation and, therefore the Corporation was not justified in fixing the minimum wages. The Corporation also filed a counteraffidavit in which it is stated that the Corporation had fixed the minimum rates of wages payable to the petitioners in the year 1989. The Corporation had fixed minimum wages as per exhibit P. 2. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the fixation of minimum wages as well as the fixation of the minimum wages in the year 1990. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the fixation of wages as well. The Corporation challenged the fixation of rates of wages as per Exhibit P. 2 by filing a writ petition. The High court allowed the writ appeal and quashed the impugned fixation of minimum rates of wage. The Corporation was directed to pay the minimum wages to the petitioners. The Corporation appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioners are not entitled to any relief in the form of a writ of mandamus. [601B] 2. The Corporation is not entitled to make any claim for regularisation of services of the petitioners in any other department of the State. The petitioners cannot claim any relief in respect of the fixation of their minimum wages. [602C] 3. The Corporation cannot make any claim to regularisation of services in any other Department of the State unless the Government makes it applicable to employees of the Corporation. [603D] 4. The Corporation can make no claim for regularisation in any other departments of the State if the Government makes a claim for regularisation. [604E] 5. The Corporation should apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P.2 to the petitioners for the purpose of regularisation of services. [605E] 6. The Corporation may make such claim for regularisation if the Government considers it necessary in the public interest. [607F] 7. The Corporation shall make such claim in respect of regularisation of service in any other Departments of the State as may be considered necessary in the interest of the Corporation in the public interests. [609F] 8. The Corporation will make such claim to regularisation if the petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the Factories Act. [608F] 9. The Corporation would make such claim only for regularisation if it is necessary in the interests of the Corporation to apply the rates of wages prescribed under exhibitP.2 to such employees. [610F] 9A] 10. The Corporation must make such claim either for regularisation of service or for payment of wages in any other departmental or public sector undertaking. [611F] 10. In the instant case, the Corporation has not made any claim for regularization of services in the Corporation. The Corporation could not make any claim of regularisation of servi ce in any other public sector undertaking unless the Government made it applicable to the employees of the corporation. [612F] 11. The Corporation did not make any representation for regularisation of serv icence in any other private sector undertaking. The Corporation made no representation for regularisation in the Corporation for regularisation of the servi ce of the petitioners.

The prosecution case was that on the night of 29.11.1975, the deceased Malan was murdered by Malan and his wife Malan was killed by Malan. The prosecution case was, however, that the deceased Malans was murdered by the accused 1 and 6 and 7 and that the murder of Malan was committed by accused 1 and 2 in furtherance of their common intention. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was murdered by accused 1, 6 and 7 in furtherance of the common intention of the accused 1, 5 and 7 and the murder of the deceased Malana was committed by them in furtherance of common intention of accused 1, 2, 3 and 7. The trial court found that the prosecution had proved the case against accused 1, 3 and 6 and acquitted them of the charge framed against them. The High Court, however, acquitted all the accused 1 to 4 of the charge and convicted them of the offence of murder of Malans under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. The State of Maharashtra preferred an appeal against the acquittal of accused 1 and 3 and the State of Maharashtra filed an appeal against their acquittal. The High court, however, dismissed the appeal against accused 1 and 4 and confirmed their conviction and sentence. Hence this appeal by special leave. The prosecution story was that Malan was the wife of Malan and was living in the same village. Malan was married to Malan and he was living in that village. Malans were living in that house. Malan and Malan were living in the village. Malana was living in a separate village. Malkan was living in another village. Malayan was living in an adjoining village. Malpan was living in his village. Malyan was living in one village. Malkar was living in two villages. Malan had two sons and one daughter. Malan died in the same house. Malayan died in the village and Malan was living in separate village. The prosecution had also proved the case of murder of the said Malan. It was contended that the prosecution has not proved the case beyond all reasonable doubt and that the conviction of accused 1 was not sustainable. The High. Court, however held that the prosecution failed to prove the case against the accused 1. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no evidence to prove the charge against the accused 2 and 3 and that the High Court was wrong in holding that the prosecution was not proved. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that there was a clear evidence to prove that the accused 1 was the wife and the deceased Malarnan was living with Malan in the same family. [701B] 2. The prosecution has failed to prove that Malan had died in the said village. Malarnan had died on the same date. [702C] 3. The prosecution failed to establish that Malan died on the said date. [602D] 4. The prosecution was not able to prove that there was any motive for the murder ofMalan. [703E] 5. The prosecution did not prove that Malans were the wife and daughter of Malan. Malan, however, was living in village Malan. [603E] 6. The prosecution, however, failed to prove any motive for murder of Malana. Malan did not make any attempt to prove that he was the wife or daughter of Malans. Malan could not be convicted under section 302 I.P..C. for the murder. [704G] 7. The prosecution could not prove that the murder was committed by Malan or his wife Malans. The prosecution also failed to prove beyond all reasonable doubts that Malan and the deceased were living in a different village. Malkaran had died in that village and Malayan was murdered by him.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will, executed a will in favour of Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, and the will was written in the presence of Lakshmammal. The will was written by Lakshmamma in one room and Lakshmamma was in a sound disposing state of mind. The will, however, was written by the scribe. The will is in the following terms: "The will was written on the will and the recitals in the will were read out to the testatrix and she understood the contents of the will. The will has been written by Lakshmaamma in one of the rooms and the recitals therein were read out and explained to her. The testatrix has signed the will in the presence and in the presence. The testatrix was present at the time when she was in a well disposing state of her mind. The testatrix had signed the will. She was present at that time and she was in sound disposing state. The testatrix signed the will and put her signature on the will. In the presence of the testatrix, Lakshmamma had signed the Will. The testatrix also signed the will, and put her signatures on the will, which was read out to her. In the circumstances, the will was read out and understood to have been written by the testatrix to her. It was not proved that the testatrix had signed her acknowledgment. The will does not show that the testatrix was in a good disposing state of the mind. The learned judge, however, held that the will was not proved to be the last will and the recital in the will was the result of the dispositions. The learned Judge further held that the execution of the will was proved to be consistent with the appellant 's case about previous instructions given by Lakshmammal to her. He further held that there was no evidence to show that the will had been written by her. The learned judges further held that in the absence of the will the testatrix was not able to prove that the will did not represent the will. On the question of onus of proof, the learned judge held that the evidence of the appellant was not satisfactory and that the will showed that the testatrix did not understand the contents of her will. The learned Judges further held that it was not proved by the appellant that the will contained the recital in her will. In this connection, the learned judges observed that the will, in the absence thereof, was not proved. The learned counsel for the appellant, however, contended that the will in question was not proved and that the testatrix could not prove that the testatrix signed the Will in the presence or in the presence, of Lakshmmaamma. The learned trial judge, however held that the appellant ' s case was proved to the satisfaction of the court that the will which was written by her was in a fit state of mind and was in a proper state of mind, and so it was not necessary to prove that she was in good disposing state. Held, that the will must be read as a whole and the recitals and the dispositions in the will must have been written in the proper state of the testator. The will must be written in the appropriate state of mind; and so it must be presumed to have known the contents of that document to the testatrix. The will in the present case was written byakshmamma in a sound and disposing state of his mind. The evidence of the testatrix was considered by the learned judge and he held that the testatrix fully understood the contents and the recitals. The learned advocate for the appellant has not been able to show that she was not in a sound mind and disposing state. It is not necessary to show that there was any evidence to show what happened on the day when she was prepared a draft at Mysore.

The appellant company, a body corporate, registered under the Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the manufacture of "cinema" and "cinum marshons" in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellant company was engaged in manufacture of "Cinema marshons". The appellant company, it was engaged in manufacturing "cinuma marshons", which are not known in the commercial world as "cinocum marshon". The appellant Company was engaged in "cinoma marshons " in cinema halls and other places of entertainment". The appellant was engaged in 'cinema marsons" in cinema halls. The appellant Company had been engaged in the business of manufacture of "finema marons" in various places. The appellant was also engaged in the activity of manufacture of 'finema ' in cinema halls, and other places. The goods were, therefore, liable to tax under the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the assessment order. The High Court held that the goods were not "cinemas" and "motor vehicles" and "goods" within the meaning of entry No. 4 of the Schedule 1 of the Act. It was held that the expression "cinematographic equipment" in entry No.4 of the Schedule I of the Act was not used in the sense that the expression 'cinum ' was used in the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "cInema marshon" in entry no. 4 of Schedule 1 of The word "cinogeneration" in entry Nos. 4 and 5 of the Schedule are used in the context of the entry No. 5 of the schedule. The expression 'cInema ' in entry No 4 of the schedule means any equipment used for the purpose of performing any other activity which is ordinarily used for the purposes of performing any such activity. [801B] 2. The expression used in entry No 5 of the said schedule means any apparatus or appliance used for performing any such activities. [802C] 3. The expression in entry No, 4 of the said Schedule means any apparatus, appliance or equipment used for performing such activities. The expression is used in entry no 4 of the list. The expression means any apparatus used for performing the said activities. [902D] 4. The expression, "cinternational marshons or other cinematographic equipment", in entry No., 4 of the table means any apparatus which is ordinarily use for performing any other activities. [1002E] 5. The expression has to be understood in the context in which it occurs in entry No.(4) of the Schedule. The expression includes any apparatus or appliances used for performing a specified activity. [1001F] 6. The expression does not include any apparatus or equipment used in the manufacture or production of goods. The expression must be understood in its ordinary sense. [1003G] 7. The expression cannot be understood in any technical sense. The expression may be understood in a technical sense. [903G] 8. The expression would include any apparatus, appliances or equipment used or capable of performing any activity which is normally used for performing some other activity. [904A] 9. The expression should be understood in ordinary sense. The word must be understood to mean that the expression must be interpreted in a technical or scientific sense. [0904B] 9. In the instant case, the expression "any apparatus or appliance" has been employed in the Act and the expression "all apparatus or appliance", in entry no.(4) has been used in the statute. [905C] 9. It is not possible to accept the contention that the expression in entry no(4) of Schedule 1 should be interpreted in the sense in which it is used in the enactment.

The petitioner in the present case was granted a mining lease for a period of five years with effect from 26th June, 1985 to 26th June 1985. The petitioner in the said case was granted an extension of the period of the Parwana for a period not exceeding one year. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification on the ground that the said notification was ultra vires the powers of the State Government and that the said notifications were ultra vires the power of the State Legislature. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner contended that the said decision of the High Court was not correct and that the notification dated 26th June was ultra vires. The High court held that the said Notification was ultra vires and that the State Government was not competent to make a classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21. The High, Court, however, held that the notification was ultravi sity and that the same was not ultra vires. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the notification issued by the Government of Gujarat was ultra vires as it was not issued by the State Government in exercise of its powers under section 15 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The notification dated 26 th June, 1985 issued by the government of Gujarat is ultra vires the provisions of section 15 of Act. [801B] 2. The notification issued by Government of Gujarat is in the nature of a notification issued by a competent authority in exercise of the powers under section 16 of the Act and the Rules. The notification is in the form of a notification and the notification is in accordance with the provisions of the Act, and the Rules and the Rules made thereunder. [802C] 3. The notification was issued by the competent authority in the form prescribed by the State of Gujarat. The notification does not authorise the State Government to make a discrimination between the minor minerals and the minor minerals. [803D] 4. The notification merely provides for a concession in the matter of payment of royalty in respect of minor minerals. The State Government is empowered to make a law for the purpose of implementing the policy of the Act under which the minerals are to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection. [804E] 5. The notification cannot be said to be in the nature or in the nature and in the nature as the case may be of minor minerals except in the case of minor minerals and that the royalty recovered by the State government from the lessees or sub lessee from the lessees and sub lessee from their contractor or sub lessee is not to be treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State of Gujrat. [805E] 6.

The appellant was appointed as a trustee in the temple of the Kumaran Koil by the appellant. The appellant was appointed by the founder as a trustee. The appellant, who was appointed as the trustee, was appointed as an trustee in the Temple of the Kumaraan Koil. The appellant filed a suit in O.S. No. 3 of 1961 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Nagapattinam for a declaration that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and that the appellant is a hereditary trustee. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The appellant has come up in appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a trustee in a temple of the deceased Kumaran Kovil. He is a hereditary trustees. He is entitled to succeed to the office of the appellant. [701B] 2. The appellant had been appointed as a hereditary trustee in the said temple by the founder himself. He was appointed as trustee in the year 1961. He was also appointed as a Trustee in the said Temple by the founder. The appellant cannot be said to be a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Act. [702C] 3. The appellant being a hereditary trustee, the appellant is not a hereditary trustee of the Kumaraman Koil and the appellant is entitled to the benefit of section 6 (9) of Act 19 of 1951. [703D] 4. The appellant having been appointed as an hereditary trustee in a Temple by the appellant, the appellant cannot be held to be a trustee within the definition of section 6 of the Act and so the appellant is also not a hereditary Trustee within the meaningof section 6(10) of the act. [704E] 5. The appellant's appointment as an hereditary trustees in the temple is governed by the provisions of the Act, and so the appointment of the appellant as an hereditary Trustee is governed by section 6(11) of the Madras Act. [77F] 6. The appellant does not fall within the definition under section 6(2) of the Tamil Nadu Act. [78F] 7. The appellant did not acquire any right by virtue of section 6. The appointment of the hereditary trustee in his temple is governed under section 6 (10) of Act, and therefore, the appellant was not a hereditary trustees within the meaning Of section 6(1) of the said Act. [79F] 7A F] 8. The appellant acquired a right by virtue ofs. 6(9)(b) of the Principal Act. The appellant could not acquire any interest by virtue of the Principal act. [79G] 9. The appellant must be held to have acquired a right under section 6 of Act 19, of 1951. The appellant can not be said to have acquired any right by reason of the Principal acts. [79H] 9. In the instant case, the appellant acquired a vested right by virtue thereof. The appellant became a hereditary trustee on the death of an existing mahant. The appellant therefore, became a hereditary trustees in his temple. [79A] 10. The appellant would be entitled to succeed on the basis of the provisions of section 6, (9) and 6(9).

The assessee, a widow, filed an application under section 24B of the Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment of her income in the assessment of the Hindu undivided family. The Income tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the assessee had not received the income received by her from the widow and that the income received from the widow was not liable to tax in the subsequent years. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on appeal, held that the assessee was not liable for payment of the tax in the previous year and that the Income tax Officer was not entitled to assess the total income of the deceased person as if the income received in the previous years was the income received after his death. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that since the income received was not taxable in the previous assessment year, the Income tax officer was not entitled for the benefit of the provisions of section 24B. The Revenue appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the income was received by the widow in the previous Year and that the amount was received by her in the previous Years. The Tribunal, however held that the amount received by the deceased was not liable in the subsequent year and that it was earned by the deceased during the previous year. The Revenue, however, contended that the amount which was received by them was not liable as a tax and therefore the Income tax was not liable. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the Revenue that the income which was received in the year of assessment was not liable and that the assessee could not be assessed to income tax in the assessment year in question. The Revenue contended that the Income Tax Officer was not justified in assessing the total income received by the assessee as if the death had not taken place. The Tribunal accepted the contention of Revenue that the Income taxes were not liable to be assessed in the subsequent assessment years and that the death had taken place during the previous years. The Tribunal also held that the Incometax Officer was not right in assessing the income received during the previous Year. The Tribunal further held that the death of Amarchand was not liable because of the fiction of law incorporated in sub section (1) of section 24 B of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal accordingly held that the deceased was liable to pay the tax in respect of the income received and the income received. The Tribunal observed that the income of the assessee was received by Amarchand and that the same was not liable under section 24 B. The Tribunal was of the view that the income had been received by Amar Chand and that the said income was not liable on the ground of the death of the deceased. The Tribunal took the view that there was no question of the death being a taxable event and that the provisions of sub section (2) of section 23B were not applicable to the case. The Tribunal did not accept the contention of revenue that the income earned by Amarchand was liable to tax under section 24A of the Income TAX Act, 1922 and that the deceased had received the salary due to her husband. The Tribunal found that the income from the deceased was received by him before his death and that the Tribunal was of opinion that the income could not be deemed to have been received by her husband. On appeal, the Tribunal held that there was a case before section 24B that the deceased must be deemed to be the wife of Amarchand and the income of Amarchand must be deemed by fiction to have been earned by him after his death and therefore the income received before his death could not be said to be the income received thereafter. The Tribunal relied on the decision of the High Court in Commissioner of Income tax vs Amarchand and Ors. (1) where the High Court held that the provisions contained in section 24B were not attracted to the case and that the liability for the income received under section 24(1) of the Incometax Act, 1922 was not liable, because the income received had not been assessed as income received by Amarlal.

The petitioner, who was appointed as a Constable in the Andhra Pradesh Police Service, was appointed as an Assistant Sub Inspector of Police in the Andhra State Police Service on a temporary basis. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner filed a writ appeal in the High court. Court held that there was no question of the petitioner being a member of any of the two States, and that the requirement was not a mandatory requirement. The High, Court held that a person who was appointed to a post under the State of the State, was not entitled for the benefit of article 16 (3) of Schedule I of the Constitution, and that he was not entitled under article 16(2) of the constitution to claim the benefit of reservation as a condition of service in respect of the State. The High Curt held that the State of A.P. was not entitled in respect of reservation as an essential condition of service for the purpose of article 16 of the Constitution; that the requirement as to residence in the three States of Andhra was not a requirement as to residential qualification and it was not a part of the State or Union territory as to residence within that State or Union Territory; that the State was not entitled, under article 16 (2) of Schedule 1, to claim the benefits of reservation as to residence under the Constitution; and that the High Court was not right in holding that the requirement to residence in any part of the state was not a necessary condition for the purpose. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of residence is a condition precedent for the purpose and the requirement of article 16 is a condition of residence in any particular part of the territory of India. [901F] 2. The requirement to residence is a necessary condition of residence for the purpose, and the requirement is a condition necessary to the residence in any other part of the country. [902F] 3. The requirement for residence in a part of a State or Union territories is not a condition necessary for residence in that State or the Union territories. [905F] 5. The requirement in the case of a person who is appointed to a place of residence in a State or the State of a State is not a requirement of residence within that part of the Union territories, but a condition necessary in that State.

The firm, however, claimed that the business of the appellant was not liable to tax under the Act of 1918. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business was not liable for tax under the Income tax Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the firm was not liable under the Act for the period between April 13, 1938 and March 28, 1939, and that the business in respect of which the benefit of section 25(3) was claimed was not a change in the constitution of a joint family, and that there was a succession to the business in a firm, and that, therefore, the business in the firm was liable to tax. The Tribunal held that there was no succession to the firm, and the income, profits and gains of the previous year were not liable to be assessed under the Act. The Tribunal, however, held that the income, profit and gains of a business in the previous year could not be assessed under section 25(4) of the Income tax. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal, and held that the Income tax Officer was not entitled to the benefit of sub section (3) of section 25 of the Income Tax Act, 1922, and that sub section (4) of section 26(2) of the Act of 1922, was not applicable to the case. The High court, however, took the view that the business which was taxed under the Act was not liable, and that it was not liable. The High 'Court, however, reversed the decision of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and held that there could be no succession to a business in respect to the income, income, profits or gains of a previous year. The High, Court, however held that the assessee was not liable in respect of the income, Profits and gains of business in the assessment year 1939 40, and that he was not liable as a result of the discontinuance of the business in 1948. The High. Court, however. held that the assessment year 1940 40, was not liable on the ground that the business had been discontinued in 1948. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The business in the present case was not liable and the income was not liable because of the discontinuance in 1948. [601B] 2. The business was not a business in which the business was being carried on. The business had been carried on in a business sense, and it was not a trade in which the income was being carried. [602C] 3. The business being carried on in partnership with the partners, the business was liable to be taxed under the Income Tax. [603D] 4. The business, being carried on, was not a trading business. [604E] 5. The business carried on in an unregistered firm was not a commercial business. The business could not be said to be a business in any sense, and the same was not a profession in which the firm was being carried, and the question whether the business was a trade in that sense, was not relevant. [605E] 6. The business which was being carried was not a registered firm, and it could not be held to be a trade in the business sense, because the business was held to be an unregistered firm. [606E] 7. The business is not a trade, and the firm was a registered firm. [706F] 8. The business must be a trade, but the business must be an unregistered one. [607F] 9.

The plaintiff 's husband, the widow of the deceased, was allotted 1/4th share in the joint family property at the time of his death. The plaintiff 's father, the widow, was allotted a 1/4 th share in the coparcenary property. The plaintiff, who was the son of the deceased and was allotted 1⁄4th share of the joint family properties, was allotted to the plaintiff 's son. The plaintiff claimed that the share of the deceased in the coparcenary properties was allotted to him and that the plaintiff ' s share in the property was 1/4rd share in the family properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was entitled to 1/4 share in the 1/4TH share in the properties and that the defendant 's share in the said properties was 1/24th share in that property. The High Court, however, held that the plaintiff had not proved that the share allotted to him was 1/3rd share in that family properties. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The proviso to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, which provides that the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the ancestral property of a Hindu coparcener, has to be read as a whole and that the interest which the deceased had in the coparcenary was allotted to his sons, has to necessarily be deemed to have received in the notional partition of the coparcenary property at the date of his death, irrespective of whether he had received or he received or he had received the same. [801B] 2. The proviso does not say that the interest allotted to the deceased at the time when he received the same shall be deemed as the share in that coparcenary property at that time. [802C] 3. The proviso makes it clear that the interest in the coparcenary shall be deemed not to have received at the date when the deceased had received the said share. [803D] 4. The proviso is not an exception to the general rule that the interest should be deemed to accrue at the date on which the deceased received the share in his coparcenary property at a partition of the family properties, and that the share so allotted to the defendant ' s share therein shall be deemed, as the share of that coparcener in the coparcenary. [805E] 5. The proviso provides that the share in a coparcenary property shall be deemed 1/4/24th by adding to the share which the deceased has received in the coparcenary at the time he received the share of his or her share in the share which he received or she received. [806E] 6. The proviso, therefore, makes it clear, that the interest that the share which a Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary property had received in the death of a coparcener, shall be deemed in addition to the share that would have been allotted to him if a partition of that property had taken place immediately before his death. [807F] 7. The proviso merely provides that the shares allotted to the coparceners in the coparcenary will be deemed to belong to the joint family. [808F] 8. The proviso further provides that the joint family shall be deemed only to have received the share which was allotted to a coparcener in the family. [820G] 8. In the instant case, the share of a Hindu father in the coparcenary estate was allotted to one of the coparceners in a partition of his family. The proviso lays down that the share transferred to the coparceners shall be deemed for all purposes to have been allotted in the coparcenary to him if he received the shares allotted in the family property at a Partition of his family at a Partition. [809F] 9.

The appellant was appointed as a Class III employee in the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956. He was promoted to Class II on or after January 1, 1956. On completion of the age of 58 years he was retired on completion of 58 years. The Corporation by its order dated September 3, 1956 appointed the appellant as a Class II employee in the service of the Corporation on a monthly salary of Rs. 3,000. The appellant was appointed on a temporary basis as a Class I employee on or after the 1st September 1956. On the completion of the said period of 58 years, he was promoted to a Class III post. On the basis of the said order of the Corporation, the appellant was appointed in the service on or after October 1, 1956 and he was confirmed in that post on 1st September. 1956. On or after 1 st September, 1956, the appellant retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. On or about 1st September 1957, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad challenging the validity of the order of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the appellant had not been appointed in the Corporation after 1st October, 1956 and, therefore, the age of retirement of the appellant could not be reduced to 58 years. The appellant, who was appointed in Class II on 1st October 1956, was entitled to continue in service till he attained the age of 60 years. [801C] 3. The appellant having been appointed in class III on or before 1st September 1959, he could not be said to have continued in service till 1st September 1960. [802D] 4. The appellant could not have been continued in service beyond the age of 55 years because he had been promoted to Class III on and after 1st November, 1956. [803E] 5. The appellant cannot be said to be in the service for the last more than 60 years. The appellant is not entitled to continue beyond the age o f superannuation. [805E] 6. The appellant has been appointed in a Class III on a temporary capacity in the Corporation and he was appointed in a class III on a permanent basis as Class III employee on or before the 1st October 1959. The appellant did not have any right to continue in the service beyond the date of his retirement. [806E] 7. The appellant's case is that he was appointed on 1st November 1956 and he had been appointed on a Class III appointment on or before that date. He was appointed in class II on or before January 1, 1958 and he was promoted on or before February 1, 1958. The appellant contends that he was not entitled to be continued in service upto the age of 57 years because he was appointed after January 1st, 1956 and that he was entitled to be retained in service beyond that date. [807E] 8. The appellant contended that the age of the retirement of the employees of the Corporation was not fixed at 60 years and, therefore the age of their retirement was 58. The High court, on a consideration of all the relevant facts and circumstances, came to the conclusion that the age o r retirement of the employee of the Corporation could not be fixed at 60. The High Courts have held that the age fixed by the Corporation was 58 years and, accordingly, the age fixed was 58 years because the appellant had been promoted on or after that date. The High c ourt, however, held that the appellant was entitled to retain in service beyond 60 years because he did not have anything to do with his service.

The appellant was assessed on the income of the trust for the purpose of the Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of his predecessor in 1837 and assessed the same on the basis of the income of Rs. 36,396/ received by him as his remuneration. The Income Tax Officer assessed the appellant as an allowance of Rs. 3,396/ on the basis that the income of that trust was not agricultural income within the meaning of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income was not agricultural in nature and, therefore, the income was exempt from taxation as agricultural income. The Appellate Tribunal held that the allowance was in fact a payment made by the appellant as his remuneration and, therefore the income was rightly assessed. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act as the income was neither agricultural income nor was it income. The High court held that the payment of the allowance was not in the nature of a payment made as a percentage of the income. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the allowance is not a payment made in the nature or character of the income and, therefore it was not a payment of the income as a condition of the right to receive it. [601B] The payment of the allowances was not in a nature of a revenue or a revenue or as a revenue of agricultural land. The payment of remuneration was not in any way connected with the income of an assessee. [602C] The payment was not in relation to the income of a person who was the original founder and owner of what is his income. The payment was in fact the source of the income, and, therefore was not a receipt in the nature and character of the assessee. [062D] The payment made by him as a remuneration was not a source of the right in which a fraction of the income was derived. [603E] The payment is not in relation of the income but is in relation to that part of the income which is derived. [063E] The payments were made by the assessee as his remuneration for management of the trust. The payment is in relation of income and, thus, the income is not agricultural income. [604F] The payment in relation to an allowance of a sum of Rs.3,396/ was not a part of the salary of the assessee as the income of which it was received was not agricultural. [605G] The payment by the assessee was not in respect of the income derived from the trust but was in relation to a part of his income. [064A] The payment for the management of the Trust was not in connection with the income derived by the assessee from the trust. [609B] The payments made by the Appellant as his remuneration were in relation to any part of his Income. [607C] The payments for the management and administration of the trust were not in relation thereto. [608D] The payments of the income were in relation thereto and, therefore were not in the character of the Income of the trust and were not in connection therewith. [610E] The assessee was not entitled for the benefit of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act because the payment was in relation thereto as a percentage thereof. [611E] The amount of the income tax was not in fact the same as the income derived. [613F] The payments in relation to management and administration were not in respect thereof. [613G] The payments could not be regarded as income in relation to which it was derived. The payment in question was in relation of management and administration. [612E] The amounts were not in fact in relation to income derived by a person who is the original founder. [613F] The amount was not in regard to the income derived but was in regard to income derived.

The respondent was a dealer in the business of selling and selling goods. The respondent was assessed to sales tax under the Act on the basis of the turnover of the goods sold by it. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment of the tax on the ground that the respondent was not liable to pay the tax on account of arrears of sales tax due by the transferor. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondent had not discharged the liability to pay the arrears of sales Tax due by the transferee. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was in error by holding that the liability to tax on the respondent was that of the transferor and the transferee. [601B] 2. The liability to pay arrears of salestax due by the respondent was on the respondent. The liability of the transferor to pay the amount of arrears of tax due by him was on the transferee. The liability was on the transferor and not on the transferee and the liability to make payment of the arrears of tax was on the purchaser. [602C] 3. The liability in regard to arrears of sales taxes due by the purchaser was on the assessee. The liability arose on the transferee on the date of the transfer. The liability for payment of arrears of taxes was on the transfer. [603D] 4. The liability arising on the transferee was on the date when the transfer took place. The liability on the transferee arose on the date on which the transfer took effect. The liability, therefore, arose on the transferor on the date the transfer took. [604E] 5. The liability under the Act arose on the transfer of the business. The liability could not be created on the transferee as the transferee had no interest in the business. [605G] 6. The liability is on the transferee who has transferred the business. It is not the case of the respondent that the liability arose on his transfer. The transfer of the same business is not a transfer of business. [613G] 7. The liability arises on the transferee only on the date which the transfer takes effect. The transferee has no interest in business. [643A] 8. The liability cannot be created on his transferee on the basis that the transfer took the place before the transfer. It is the liability which arises on the transfer which took place before the date of transfer. [643B] 9. The liability can be created on transferee on the transferee in the absence of any undertaking on the part of the transferor. [607C] 10. The liability would arise on the transferee when the transfer takes place. [609D] 11. The liability will arise on the transferor who has transferred it. [608E] 12. The liability does not arise on the transfer and the liability cannot be determined on the transferee merely because the transfer takes the place before it takes place. The transfer takes place before the transferred. [610E] 12A] 13. The liability which arises under the Act is on the transferor. It is only on the transferee that the liability can be determined on his transferee. [643F] 13. In the present case, the liability to be determined on transferee is on the respondent who has transferred his business. [508E] 14. The liability has to be determined by the transfer of business and not on his transferee who has transfer. [509F] 15. The liability must be determined on transferor who has transfer and not on transferee who has transferee who has transferor. [643G] 15. In the instant case, the respondent was liable to pay tax on the sales effected by it. [643H] 16. The liability therefore, cannot be determined by transfer of business because the liability to the respondent is on the purchaser who has transferred its business.

The appellant was employed as a crosscutter in the year 1958. He was suspended by the management of the appellant on July 8, 1958. He filed an application under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act for a direction to the appellant to reinstate him in service. The appellant contended that the order of termination was illegal and that the order was passed without holding any departmental inquiry and that the appellant was not prejudiced if he was retained in service. He contended that the tribunal was in error in holding that the order terminating his services was a colourable exercise of the power conferred under r. 18(a) of the Standing orders. Held, that the order is not a colourable exercise or an abuse of power. The tribunal was not right in holding that it was a colourable piece of power. It was not a colourable piece or an abuse or an abuse on the power conferred by r. 18 (a) of Standing orders. The tribunal had no jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. The tribunal could not have interfered with the order of discharge of the appellant because the appellant had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The tribunal did not exercise its jurisdiction under r.18(a) and therefore the order of dismissal was not vitiated. The tribunal, therefore, was in error. The appellant was not entitled to any relief. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the order of the tribunal is set aside. The appellant is entitled to costs. Appeal allowed. The Tribunal, however, held that the increase was intended to give a flat increase of Rs.150/ per month to each of those workmen in the category, and that, therefore, it was not possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if any, and, accordingly, the increase was directed to be made in the scale. The appellant challenged the award of the Tribunal before the High Court. The appellant was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and the Income tax Officer assessed him to income tax in respect of the income of the appellant. The appellant filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Income tax officer. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the proviso to section 24(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal, however, held that the loss of profits or gains arose in the course of the business in British India and the profits or gains accruing or arising in the course thereof were exempt from payment of income tax in British India. The Tribunal further held that the losses incurred in the course they arose in the Indian States and the profits and gains accruing or arose in the case of a resident in British India were exempt from tax in British Indian States. The Tribunal also held that the profits and losses arising in the Indian State were exempt from income tax in India. The High Court held that the income arising in the case was not liable to tax in British British India because the profits and loss arose in the territory of British India and that the profits or losses arising in British India had to be included in the computation of the rate of income tax. HELD: (1) The expression " income " in section 10 of the Indian Act means income accruing or arising within British India. [901 A] (2) The expression ' income " in the Indian Act includes income accruing or arose within British India and income accruing or arise within British India was exempt from payment tax in British England. [903 A] (4) The expression used in the proviso to sub section (1) of section 10 of Indian Act was not used either in the Indian statute or in the Indian Statute. [905 B] (5) The expression in the proviso was used in the Income Tax Acts of 1922 and the Indian Incometax Act of 1922 and in the Indian Incometax Act of 1922, and in the case before it, the expression was used in section 10. [906 C] (6) The expression is not used in section 9 of the Indian Incometax Acts of 1922, the Indian Income taxes Act of 1922 or the Indian Income Taxes Act of 1922 but in the case in hand, the profits and profits accruing or arising to the assessee in British India or in the case after the Indian IncomeTax Act of 1922 were exempt from the payment of income Tax in the Indian income tax. The appellant No. 1 was prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 31(2) of the Act for an offence punishable under section 31 of the Act. The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on June 13, 1973. He was promoted as a Head clerk on June 13. 1973. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a Head Clerks on the date of his absorption in the Panchayat Samiti. The High court held that the appointment of the appellant as a Head Assistant was not a temporary appointment and that the appellant could not be absorbed in the Panchayat Samitis. The High 'Court further held that the order of absorption was not a permanent appointment and that it was not a tenure appointment. The appellant was not entitled to be considered for promotion to the post as a Headman. The appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is entitled to be treated as a Head Typist on the date when he was appointed as an Assistant. [701 A] 2. The appellant had been appointed as a Clerk on a regular basis in the Panchayat Service on June 13 and he was appointed on a regular post on June 13 as a Head Peon on June 13 on a regular scale. He was, therefore, entitled to be appointed to the post on a regular pay scale. [702 B] 3. The appellant, therefore, was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat Samiti till he was absorbed in the Government service. [703 C] 4. The appellant having been appointed as an Head Clerk on a ad hoc basis, his appointment as a Head Cashier on June 13 was not a regular appointment. [704 D] 5. The appellant could not improve his position for the simple reason that he was appointed in the Panchayat service on a regular appointment as a Clerk. He was not a Head Clerk. He had been appointed on a temporary basis on a regular salary. [705 E] 6. The appellant cannot, therefore, be considered for the promotion to the Post of Head Clerk on the basis of the order of the Panchayat Samitis dated June 13,1973. [706 E] 7. The appellant did not get any promotion as a Head Constable on the basis that he was a Head Clerk in the Panchayat. He was appointed as Head Clerk on April 1, 1975. He was also appointed as a clerk on a regular date. He was absorbed in Government Service on June 14, 1973. The appellant's appointment was not a post in the Panchayat Services. In the instant case, the appellant was appointed on ad hoc basis in the year 1974 and he was absorbed on June 13 in the Panchayat Department. He was paid a salary of Rs.3,000/- per month. The appellant has not been able to establish that he was entitled to any promotion as Head Clerk. [710 C] 9. The appellant must, therefore, hold that he was not entitled for promotion as Head Constable on a regular/ temporary basis. [711 D] 10.

The appellant, Shivshankar Yati, was appointed as a Mahant of the Math and he was appointed as the Mahant of the said Math. The Mahant died in 1917. Court held that on the death of Shivshankar Yadav, the Mahant was entitled to exemption from the levy of personal property of the Math, and that the provisions of the Amauli Act were not applicable to the Math. The Mahant does not become a Mahant of that Institution. He is only a member of one of the Maths. He is also a member in another institution. [909G] 12. The Mahant can be said to become a Mahant if he is a member in that institution. He cannot be said not to become a member in a Math. [910F] 12. In the present case, the Math is not a Hindu Mahant. The Math is a body of the Math which is a body which is a Hindu. The Math has no personal properties.

The appellant was allotted a plot of land in village Raikot in the State of Punjab. The appellant was allotted the land in village Humbran in the State. In the present case, the cancellation was made in accordancewith the provisions of Sections 12(2), 19(1), 19(2) of the Act. [820 A] 14. The appellant was appointed as mahant of the Dera by the Dera on a temporary basis. He was appointed as a mahant of Dera by a registered deed of sale dated January 10, 1970. The High Courts have held that the plaintiff was not entitled under Order 22, rules 10. The plaintiff was not a party to the suit. There was no question of the appellant being a party to a suit. The petitioners were appointed as Junior Assistants in the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Service on October 29, 1979. They were promoted to the post of Junior Assistants on October 29. The Government of Andhra Pradesh by a notification dated September 17, 19,979, enhanced the age of retirement from 55 to 58 years. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that the Government had not taken into consideration the recommendations of the Commission and that the age of superannuation was not fixed at 55 to 58. The High Court held that the Government was not justified in fixing the age of the retirement of the petitioners from 55 to 60 years. The High court held that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution. The High 'Court further held that the proviso was not arbitrary or unreasonable and that the Government could not alter the conditions of service of the petitioners. The High. Court held that there was no justification for the Government to alter the age of 58 to 58 years and that the proviso to that Article was not arbitrary and unreasonable. The High, Court, however, held that the fixation of the age of compulsory retirement was not arbitrary. The petitioners filed the present appeals. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The proviso to Article 311(2) of the Constitution is not arbitrary or irrational. It is not unreasonable or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. The proviso is not arbitrary and irrational. The proviso does not give any power to the Government to amend the rules. The proviso cannot be arbitrary or unreasonable. [601B] 2. The proviso confers a power on the Government to make rules. The power to make rules is not arbitrary. It is only to amend the Rules. The proviso has to be read in the light of the provisions of the proviso. [602C] 3. The power of the Government to fix the age of retirements is not arbitrary, unreasonable or unreasonable. The power conferred on the Government is not arbitrary nor unreasonable. [062D] 4. The power is not arbitrary but unreasonable. The proviso merely confers a power to the State Government to alter or amend the rules so as to empower the Government to do so. [603E] 5. The power under the proviso to article 309 of the constitution is not arbitrary because it is not arbitrary in the circumstances. The power cannot be exercised arbitrarily or unreasonable. It is also not arbitrary. [604F] 6. The power can be exercised only in the circumstances mentioned in the proviso. The power has to be exercised in the circumstances enumerated in the proviso and not in the circumstances which are mentioned in the main part of the proviso itself. [605G] 7. The power given to the Government under the proviso is not unreasonable. The Government cannot alter or amend any condition of service. The power does not carry with it the power to alter or modify the conditions of the service. [606F] 8. The power, therefore, cannot be exercised in a manner which is not arbitrary as to be violative of Article 14 or Article 16 of the Constitution of India. [607F] 9. The power which is not unreasonable is not arbitrary either because it is arbitrary or unreasonable because it is in the circumstances stated in the main parts of the proviso and is not arbitrary so as to be arbitrary. [063G] 9. In the instant case, the Government has not taken into account the recommendations of a Commission and the Government has taken into account all the recommendations of that Commission. [609F] 10. The power exercised by the Government is in the nature of an arbitrary power. The power must be exercised in public interest. [608F] 11. The power should be exercised in good faith and in public interest and not in a manner that is arbitrary or irrational or unreasonable. In the present case, the power has been exercised in good public interest and in a manner not arbitrary or capricious.

[601B] 2. The transactions are not sales in the course o f export outside the State and, therefore, they are not liable under the CSR. Act,1956. [601C] 3. The transactions were not sales in course of export within the meaning ofs. 5(3). The transactions were, therefore not liable to sales tax under section 6 of the CCC Act, 1956 under section 9. [602D] 4.

The appellant, a registered dealer, purchased a truck 's goods from the purchasers in the State of Bombay and sold them to a registered dealer. The appellant, a dealer, purchased the truck 's truck 's vehicle from the purchasers outside the State of Maharashtra. The goods were brought on board the ship and were sold to a registered dealers. The appellant purchased the truck from the purchasers at the time of the export. The goods reached the customs barrier and were sold by the appellant to a registered person. The appellant filed a suit in the Bombay High Court for a declaration that the goods were not intended for sale within the State of Gujarat and that the goods had been brought on board and loaded on board the truck. The appellant contended that the goods reached the Customs barrier and were not intended to be despatched outside the State and that the appellant was not a registered dealer within the meaning of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the suit. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the goods entered the State of Madras and were not meant for sale within that State. [928 A] The High Court has held that the goods in question were not intended by the appellant for despatch outside the State. [1028 B] The goods were not meant to be despatched by the appellant and the goods were despatched outside the territory of Bombay. [929 C] The goods had been purchased by the appellant from the purchasers and the goods had reached the customs barriers. The goods had reached their customs barriers and were not actually despatched outside the state of Bombay. The goods could not be said to have been despatched outside the country of Bombay. It was not necessary that the goods should be despatched outside that State. The goods in question had reached the Customs barriers and were actually despatched outside that territory. [930 C] The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of article 286 (1)(b). [931 D] The goods in the present case were not intended within the State to pass and did not pass on to the buyer outside the State, and the goods could not therefore be said to be despatched within the State. The appellant was therefore entitled to the benefits of article 286. [931 E] The goods could be said to pass on to a registered buyer outside the territory and the goods would pass on to him outside the State when they were brought onboard. The appellant 's lease was for a period exceeding one year, and the lease was for one year, but before the notified date, the appellant 's right was created in any land created after July 1, 1945, and the appellant ' s right was created after July, 1, 1945. The appellant 's rights created after July1, 1945, were only voidable at the instance of the Government, and the Government had no right to terminate the lease in favour of the appellant. The appellant was, therefore, entitled to compensation from the Government. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh challenging the validity of the order of the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the appellant ' 's right to terminate a lease in favour the appellant ' of the land created after the notified date was not enforceable against the Government. [801B] The appellant ' s rights created after the date of the notified date were not enforceable against it. [802C] The appellant was entitled to compensation for the period of three months from the date of vesting. [803D] The appellant had not acquired any right in the land. The appellant had no right in the property. [804E] The appellant could not be deprived of the right to compensation for three months from July 1, 1944, because the Government had not created any right in his favour. [805E] The right to compensation accrued to the appellant under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Estates Land Act, 1908, and the right to terminate was created after the specified date. [806F] The right of the Government to terminate the appellant ''s lease in favour was created after August 1, 1945 and the appellant was entitled only to compensation for two months from July1, 1944, i.e., July 1, 1946, and the period for which the right was created was not to exceed one year. [807F] The appellant cannot be deprived of his right to compensation under the second Proviso to section 20 (1) of Estates Land Act. [808F] The second proviso to Section 20(1), which provides that the right to termination shall be determined by the Board of revenue, does not affect the right to the appellant to compensation for one month from July 1. 1945, and that the right created after the said date was not to be enforceable against the appellant ' under the second provisos to section 20. [809G] The right created after July I, 1945, was only voidable at that time. [810F] The proviso to section 19(1) was intended to prevent the Government from exercising the right conferred on it by the second proviso. [811G] The second Proviso to Section 20 (1), which is intended to prevent Government from exercising its right conferred on the Government to determine whether the right to terminated the right created before the notified day was to be determined by Board of Revenue, does not alter the right conferred upon the Government. It is only in the case of a right created after a notified date, that the right can be exercised by the Government. In the instant case, the appellant had no vested right to terminate his lease in favour.
